abstract: Chronic stress is associated with altered adaptation to threat, yet its effects on aversive learning under varying threat predictability and controllability remain unclear. Thirty participants with chronic stress and thirty healthy controls completed a task to learn how well visual cues predicted upcoming electric shocks (predictability) and whether correct predictions of shocks could reduce shock intensity (controllability). We found that, for controllable conditions, accuracy was similar across varying degrees of predictability in the chronic stress group, whereas accuracy in the healthy control group was highest in highly predictable blocks. The chronic stress group responded more slowly than controls and their skin conductance responses were generally lower and indistinguishable across predictability and controllability. We used a computational model to estimate subjective uncertainty and related these estimates to behavioural responses and skin conductance. Modelling showed that controllability shaped uncertainty differently across groups. In chronic stress, with control, subjective stress reflected uncertainty about likely outcomes, reaction time reflected changing outcome probabilities, and skin conductance reflected unexpected outcomes. Without control, subjective stress reflected unexpected outcomes, reaction time uncertainty about likely outcomes, and skin conductance both unexpected outcomes and outcome uncertainty. In healthy controls, subjective stress reflected changing outcome probabilities with control and outcome uncertainty without control, whereas skin conductance showed the reverse pattern, and reaction time reflected likely outcomes only under control. Together, these findings indicate less adaptation in chronic stress, reflected in reduced modulation of reaction time by controllability and skin conductance by predictability and controllability, alongside altered uncertainty associations across response domains.
